title: The Cloud's Secret
markdown:
The sun poked its bright face over the pointy peaks and painted Callum’s ceiling in pinks and oranges. He blinked awake. A perfect morning! Absolutely perfect! Then he looked at the sky, and the sky was a peculiar puzzle of blues and greys.

“Look, Birch!” Callum leaped out of bed. His feet landed with a soft thump. He dashed to the window and squashed his nose against the cool glass. Outside, fluffy white clouds drifted like scoops of vanilla ice cream, the sort you could picnic under without a worry. But then there were the others. Big, dark, lumpy ones. Heavy giants, huddled together, sharing hushed secrets. They looked so full, so promising—or maybe threatening, packed with water just waiting to fall.

A frantic whiz and a blur of brown fur zipped past the open window. Birch the squirrel landed on the sill, bushy tail twitching like a question mark made of fluff. “Can’t gather acorns today!” he chattered, tiny claws scratching the paint. “Those big, grumpy clouds are blocking the sun. They’re making everything damp and gloomy. Why don’t they just drift away like the others? They’re just sitting there, making me wait!”

Callum tapped his chin. His busy brain buzzed. “That’s a good question, Birch. A really good one. The white ones seem light and happy, just drifting. But those dark ones look heavy. So heavy! What makes a cloud heavy enough to actually rain?”

A gentle “Hello, Callum! Hello, Birch!” floated up from the garden, like a sweet melody on the breeze. Mrs. Rowan was already among her prize pumpkins, hands dusted with rich dark soil, orange skins promising autumn.

Callum dashed downstairs. Birch scrambled after him, claws finding purchase on every step. “Mrs. Rowan,” Callum blurted, breathless, “why do some clouds rain buckets and others just float like balloons? What’s the big difference?”

Mrs. Rowan chuckled, a warm rumbling sound. Her kind eyes crinkled. “Ah, a capital question. You’ve noticed something truly wonderful. Come closer, both of you.” She led them to a neat row of buckets and watering cans. Some were empty and glinting. Others held shimmering rainwater. “Clouds are tiny, tiny droplets of water, floating high up. Think of them like little water bubbles, billions and billions of them, all dancing together.”

She picked up an empty blue bucket. “When there aren’t many droplets, or they’re spread far apart, the cloud stays light and floats. Like those fluffy white ones, with a gentle breeze to push them.”

Then she lifted a sturdy green watering can, half-full. “But sometimes more and more tiny water droplets gather. They bump into each other, and when they bump, they start to stick. They cling together, making the cloud bigger, and heavier. It gathers more and more water, until it simply can’t hold it all anymore.” She tipped the can, and a perfect splash landed on a thirsty pumpkin leaf. “Then, splish, splash, plop! The water falls down. We call that rain.”

Callum’s eyes widened. Billions of tiny water bubbles bumping and sticking, growing heavier. “So the dark clouds are just… super-full?”

“Precisely.” Mrs. Rowan beamed, smile bright as a sunflower. “They’re packed to the brim. They’ve done their gathering, and now it’s time to release their gift.”

Callum’s gadget-fixing brain buzzed. He raced back upstairs, Birch chattering questions behind him. He grabbed a clear plastic tube, a battery-powered fan, and a handheld mister. With nimble fingers he attached the fan to one end of the tube. He put a bit of water at the bottom, then used the mister to create a fine, misty fog that swirled inside.

“Watch this, Birch!” Callum grinned. He flicked the switch. A gentle breeze blew, keeping the mist dispersed, swirling like tiny specks of dust. “See? The mist stays up, spread out, like little dancers. Like those light, white clouds. They’re not heavy. They’re just happy to float.”

Birch peered in, whiskers twitching. “It just floats around! Like magic!”

“But what if we slow down the air, and let the mist gather and get really thick?” Callum adjusted a dial, slowing the fan. Then, with a puff, he added more mist. Inside the tube the fog thickened, growing denser and darker. The tiny droplets bumped and clung. The mist grew so thick it looked cloudy. Suddenly a few tiny drops appeared on the inside of the tube, trickling down like mini-waterfalls.

“Whoa!” Birch yelped, jumping back. “It’s raining inside the tube! You made it rain!”

“When the water droplets in the cloud gather and get too heavy, they fall as rain,” Callum said, voice ringing. “It’s just like this tube getting too full of mist. The dark clouds are just super-full clouds. They’ve gathered a great big load of water, and they’re ready to share it.”

From her garden, Mrs. Rowan nodded. The pumpkin leaf still shone where the watering-can splash had landed. Callum looked up again and saw more than fluffy shapes. He saw a system, a cycle of water. The puffy white ones held water loosely. The dark ones were bursting with it. Light clouds float. Full clouds fall.

Birch, already eyeing a patch of sunshine pushing between the giants, gave a happy flick of his tail. “More acorns, less waiting!”

Callum grinned, mind buzzing with ideas for new gadgets. He left the tube on the sill, still beading with its tiny homemade rain, and wondered what else the sky was gathering up there, droplet by droplet, while he and Birch waited for the sun.
characters: Callum (a quicksilver gadget fixer), Birch (an acorn-sorting squirrel), Mrs. Rowan (a soil-dusted gardener)
